722.title: The birth-stories of Nanak
722.hook: janamsakhis are collections of Nanak's life-stories written down from the 1600s onward
722.howItsDone: Sikh families and gurdwara teachers retell sakhis of Guru Nanak from the janamsakhis, especially to children and on gurpurabs, as stories that carry the Guru's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabad, and your line, servants of the word. Did you thank the person who passed something good on to you? Day seven hundred twenty-two.

A boy sent to market with money and told to strike a good bargain, who comes home with empty hands. A young man who goes into a river and is given up for lost. A traveler who lies down with his feet the wrong way and is scolded for it. Pictures like these are how some children first meet Guru Nanak. The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't tell these stories. They come from somewhere else: old books of stories about his life. Today: the birth-stories of Nanak.
screen: `A BARGAIN, A RIVER, THE WRONG WAY.` → `PICTURES CHILDREN GROW UP WITH.` → `FROM OLD BOOKS OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Janam is birth. A sakhi is one story, one episode. Put them together and you get the name of a whole kind of book: the janamsakhi, a collection of sakhis about Guru Nanak's life, from his birth to his passing. Here's the first thing to know. Guru Nanak's own words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, but that book doesn't tell his life story. It's hymns, not biography. So the stories of his childhood, his travels, his meetings with holy men and kings, come to us through tellers: Bhai Gurdas, whose vars we've just been reading, and the janamsakhis, written down after his lifetime, tradition says from what his Sikhs remembered and retold. Second thing: there isn't one janamsakhi. There are several traditions of them, each with its own shape and its own tellers, and the same story can come out differently in each. Over the next few days we'll meet them one at a time. Third, and this is the heart of it: a janamsakhi isn't trying to be a modern biography, with checked dates and footnotes. It's devotional. Each sakhi is told to carry something: a teaching about truth, about the Name, about who counts as holy. Some sakhis include miracles; others are plain and human. Historians read them carefully, sorting what may be early memory from what grew later. Sikhs read them for what they teach, and some readers do both at once. Neither reading cancels the other. That's why our line today isn't stories that are facts. It's stories that carry truth. A sakhi can be weighed by a historian and still carry something true to the listener.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one sakhi. If you have a book of Guru Nanak's stories, or a site you trust, find one short sakhi and read it slowly before the sit. If not, take one of the pictures from the start: the boy who came home from market with empty hands. Then sit with it. Don't ask yet whether it happened exactly that way. Ask what it's carrying. What is the story trying to hand you? Let one answer come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when it does. The bell holds the time.
The birth-stories of Nanak. The janamsakhis: collections of sakhis, stories, of Guru Nanak's life, written down after his lifetime, each told to carry a teaching.
Your line: stories that carry truth. Today, when you hear a story told, ask what it's carrying before you ask if every detail is right. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

723.title: The Puratan tradition
723.hook: one old family of janamsakhis, valued by historians for its early material
723.howItsDone: Scholars of Sikh history read the Puratan janamsakhis alongside other traditions, while gurdwara teachers draw sakhis such as the river story from them for katha and for children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janamsakhi, and your line, stories that carry truth. Did you catch what a story was carrying before you checked the details? Day seven hundred twenty-three.

An old house, renovated many times. New kitchen, new windows, a porch someone added. But go down to the basement and there's a stretch of stone wall, rough and uneven, from when the house was first built. A builder will run a hand along it and say: that's the original. Everything else rests on it. Yesterday we learned there isn't one janamsakhi but several families of them. Historians go looking for the stone wall in the basement. Today: Puratan.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, RENOVATED.` → `ROUGH STONE IN THE BASEMENT.` → `THAT'S THE ORIGINAL.`

segments.voice: Puratan is a Punjabi word for old. This family of janamsakhis carries that name, the old ones, and historians value it for its early material about Guru Nanak's life. It isn't one book with one author. It's a group of related manuscripts telling the stories in much the same way. What makes it feel old? Some readers describe it as plainer than later tellings. The stories are spare. They move quickly. There's less decoration around them, and the Guru's own hymns are woven into the scenes. Take the river story, one of the pictures from yesterday's opening. Nanak goes down to the river to bathe and doesn't come back. His family and friends search, and fear the worst. When he returns, the Puratan tradition has him say: there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman. Sikh teachers often explain those words as a call to look past the labels people fight over, toward the One who made them all, not a rejection of anyone's faith. A historian reading that story isn't trying to disprove it. They're asking a different question: which parts of the telling are oldest, closest to the people who knew Nanak, and which grew around it later? The Puratan tradition is where historians often start that work. And here's the gentle part. Calling something the old telling doesn't make the later tellings worthless. A renovated house is still a home. But when you want to know how the house began, you go to the stone.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what's oldest in your story. Use the sit to go down to the basement of one memory. Choose someone you've known a long time: a parent, a friend, a place you've lived. Now go past everything you know about them today, back to the very first picture you have. Where were you standing? What was the light like? What did they say, if anything? That first picture is the stone wall. Notice how much has been built on top of it since, and that it's still there, holding it up. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you reach it. The bell holds the time.
Puratan, the old family of janamsakhis, plain and spare, where historians look for early material about Guru Nanak's life.
Your line: the old telling. Today, when someone you know well comes to mind, look for the first picture underneath. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

724.title: The Bala tradition
724.hook: a popular tradition tells the stories through Bhai Bala, a companion historians discuss
724.howItsDone: Some Sikh homes and gurdwaras display paintings of Guru Nanak with Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, and sakhis from the Bala tradition are still retold, while historians read them alongside older tellings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Puratan, and your line, the old telling. Did you try telling your own story the plain way first? Day seven hundred twenty-four.

"I was there." Three words, and listeners lean in. A story told by a stranger is information. A story told by someone who walked the road beside the hero is something else. You can hear the dust on their shoes. Some Sikh homes have a painting of Guru Nanak seated with two companions: Bhai Mardana with his rabab, and a second man, Bhai Bala. That second figure belongs to a whole family of janamsakhis told in his voice. Today: Bala.
screen: `I WAS THERE.` → `NANAK WITH TWO COMPANIONS.` → `A STORY IN BALA'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Bala janamsakhis present themselves. Bhai Bala, a companion of Guru Nanak on his travels, sits with the second Guru, Guru Angad, and tells what he saw. The stories come in that frame: told by a friend. It's a warm frame, and the Bala tellings are popular. They're fuller than the Puratan stories we met yesterday, with more detail, more conversation, and more wonders. Now the careful part, because historians discuss Bala. They ask whether a companion named Bala was really with Nanak on his travels. Some think the Bala frame was added later, to give the stories a witness. Others keep the question open. Sikhs differ on this too. Some hold Bhai Bala dear as a real companion. Others read the Bala janamsakhis with more caution, and prefer older tellings for history. Both groups take Guru Nanak seriously; they're asking different questions of the same stories. So what can we say for sure? That the frame matters. A story told as if by a friend asks to be trusted the way you trust a friend. That's a gift, and it's also a responsibility, because the friend's voice can carry things that grew later. The Bala tradition shows how a telling gets its warmth. Yesterday's tradition shows how a telling stays close to the stone. Sikh readers have kept both.
screen: `BALA TELLS GURU ANGAD WHAT HE SAW.` · `FULLER, WARMER, MORE WONDERS.` · `WAS BALA THERE? HISTORIANS ASK.` · `A FRIEND'S VOICE IS A GIFT AND A TRUST.` · then, large: `TOLD BY A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell a story you heard as a child. Use the sit to bring one back. A story a parent, grandparent, teacher or older cousin told you, maybe about your family, maybe about a saint or a hero. Hear it in their voice first, the way they told it. Then notice what their voice added: the pauses, the warmth, the bits they lingered on. Some of that is the best part. Some of it might not be history. Hold both without throwing either away. Later today, if you can, tell it to someone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the person who told it to you. The bell holds the time.
Bala, the companion in whose voice the Bala janamsakhis are told, his place in Nanak's travels still discussed by historians.
Your line: told by a friend. Today, notice whose voice a story reaches you in, and how much that voice makes you trust it. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

725.title: Miharban's telling
725.hook: a janamsakhi from the line of Prithi Chand, more reflective, full of discourse
725.howItsDone: Scholars of Sikh history read Miharban's janamsakhi alongside the other traditions, mindful of its origin in the line of Prithi Chand, and some draw on its discourses on Guru Nanak's hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bala, and your line, told by a friend. Whose voice did a story reach you in, and did it change how much you trusted it? Day seven hundred twenty-five.

Families have them: the uncle who fell out with everyone over the will, years ago. Nobody quite forgives him. And yet, when the old photos come out, he's the one who remembers the names, the places, what grandfather used to say at the table. You'd rather not need him. But he kept the old papers, and he's thought hard about them. Sikh history has a telling of Guru Nanak's life that comes from a line like that. Today: Miharban's telling.
screen: `THE UNCLE WHO FELL OUT WITH EVERYONE.` → `HE STILL REMEMBERS THE NAMES.` → `A TELLING FROM A RIVAL LINE.`

segments.voice: Start with the family. Prithi Chand was the elder brother of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. When Guru Ram Das chose Arjan as the next Guru, Prithi Chand did not accept it, and his line set itself up apart. Sikh tradition remembers them as rivals to the Gurus. Miharban was Prithi Chand's son, and a janamsakhi comes down under his name. Now the book itself. It doesn't read like the plain Puratan stories or the warm, wonder-filled Bala ones. It's reflective. A sakhi sets the scene, and then the telling stops to talk: a discourse, a gosht, in which Guru Nanak's own hymns are explained in the setting of the story. It reads less like a storyteller and more like a teacher thinking aloud. So how do Sikhs read a book from that line? Carefully, and not all in the same way. Some keep their distance from it because of where it came from. Some historians and readers take it seriously as one more early witness, and value its long reflections on Nanak's hymns. Neither group pretends the family quarrel didn't happen. Here's the lesson in it. A telling from someone you'd rather not agree with can still add something: a detail, a reading, a question. Taking it in isn't the same as taking their side. And every telling adds something of its teller too, which is exactly why it's worth knowing who the teller was.
screen: `PRITHI CHAND, GURU ARJAN'S ELDER BROTHER.` · `MIHARBAN, HIS SON, AND HIS TELLING.` · `A SAKHI, THEN A DISCOURSE.` · `READ CAREFULLY, AND DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `EVERY TELLING ADDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone you disagree with. Use the sit to bring one person to mind. Not someone dangerous: just someone whose views or choices you'd rather not share. A relative, a coworker, a voice you usually scroll past. Now ask one honest question of yourself: what might they know or notice that I don't? Let one possibility come. You don't have to agree with it. You only have to hear it. If you get the chance today, listen to them for a minute longer than usual. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.

726.title: The illustrated janamsakhi
726.hook: the B40 janamsakhi of 1733 comes with paintings of each sakhi
726.howItsDone: Paintings of sakhis from manuscripts such as the B40 janamsakhi are reproduced in books and exhibitions, and Sikh families and teachers use illustrated sakhis to tell Guru Nanak's stories to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miharban's telling, and your line, every telling adds. Did you give one view you'd usually dismiss a full hearing? Day seven hundred twenty-six.

A child on a parent's lap with a picture book, too young to read. They can't follow a word on the page, but they know the story anyway, because they know the pictures. Here's the wolf. Here's the door. Point, and the story comes back. This week we've met janamsakhis as words: plain ones, warm ones, reflective ones. Today, one that also speaks in pictures. It's known by a short, odd name: B40. Today: the illustrated janamsakhi.
screen: `A PICTURE BOOK ON A LAP.` → `POINT, AND THE STORY COMES BACK.` → `A JANAMSAKHI KNOWN AS B40.`

segments.voice: B40 is a janamsakhi manuscript, and what sets it apart in this week's lessons is simple: its sakhis come with paintings. Turn a page and there's the story in words. Beside it, the same story in color. Look at how the paintings work. Guru Nanak is there in scene after scene, and you learn to find him the way the child finds the wolf. When his companion Mardana is there, look for the rabab, the stringed instrument the stories say he played while the Guru sang. Around them, the people of each story: holy men, kings, villagers, travelers. The paintings don't try to show everything in the text. They pick a moment, the meeting, the question, the turn, and hold it still. That's a choice, and it's a kind of reading. Whoever painted a sakhi had to decide what the story was really about, and paint that. Now think about who a book like this served. A page of writing speaks only to someone who can read it. A painting speaks to anyone in the room. Gather round, point, and the story comes back, even for the child, even for the neighbor who never learned the script. In that sense, the pictures are tellers too, standing next to the words. And for us today, they're a window onto how Sikhs of their time imagined Guru Nanak: what he wore, how he sat, who was with him. Not a photograph, but a picture of devotion.
screen: `EACH SAKHI WITH A PAINTING.` · `FIND NANAK, FIND MARDANA.` · `THE PAINTER PICKS ONE MOMENT.` · `A PICTURE SPEAKS TO ANYONE.` · then, large: `STORIES IN PICTURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old painting. If you can, find one before the sit: a painting of Guru Nanak from an old manuscript, or any old painting at all, on your phone or on a wall. Then look at it, slowly, the whole time. First, find the main figure. Then the people around him. Then ask: which moment did the painter choose, and why that one? Let your eyes go to the corners, the small things, the hands. If you can't find one, picture a scene from a sakhi you know, and decide which single moment you'd paint. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
The illustrated janamsakhi. B40, a janamsakhi manuscript whose sakhis come with paintings: the story told twice, in words and in color.
Your line: stories in pictures. Today, if you tell someone a story, give them one clear picture to hold it by. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

727.title: How to read a sakhi
727.hook: a sakhi is not a news report; it carries truth in the shape of a story
727.howItsDone: Sikh teachers and kathakars tell sakhis of Guru Nanak's life to draw out a teaching, and they treat the Guru Granth Sahib as the measure any sakhi must agree with.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the illustrated janamsakhi, and your line, stories in pictures. Did one old painting hold your eye long enough to tell you something? Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

Did it really happen? That's the question a lot of us carry into an old story, the way we'd carry it into a headline. Who saw it? Where's the proof? Was there a camera? This week we've met the janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak: the old telling, the friend's telling, Miharban's telling, the painted pages. And across the next stretch of days they'll hand us oil that goes cool, bitter fruit made sweet, and a land of enchantment. So before we open any more of them, a tool for the road. Today: sakhi.
screen: `DID IT REALLY HAPPEN?` → `A HEADLINE QUESTION.` → `A TOOL FOR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: A sakhi is a story of the Guru's life, told and retold by the people who loved him. It isn't a news report. It carries truth in the shape of a story. So the first question to ask it isn't did this happen. It's what does it know. Practice on one we've already met in the Puratan telling. In the janamsakhis, Nanak, a grown man working at the storehouse, goes down to the river near Sultanpur to bathe, and doesn't come back. His friends search the banks. Tradition says that after days he returns, sits in silence, and when he finally speaks, his first words are these: there is no Hindu, and there is no Musalman. Now read it slowly, with three questions. First: what happens? A man goes under the water and comes up changed. Second: what does the Guru's own word say? Here we set the sakhi beside the Guru Granth Sahib, which opens with One: one Creator. Some readers hear in that One something deeper than the names people fight over. Third: what does the story know? It knows that this teaching came from somewhere deeper than a debate. It came out of the river, out of an encounter, and Nanak came back from it with a message for both of his neighbors at once. Sikhs hold the sakhis in more than one way. Some take the wonders just as they're told. Others read them as pictures of a truth too big for plain sentences. Readers on both sides of that line can still ask the same question. And here's a test that keeps a sakhi honest: if a story seems to teach something the Guru's own hymns would never say, Sikh teachers say the hymns win. The bani is the measure. The sakhi is the lamp you carry to it.
screen: `NOT A NEWS REPORT.` · `THE RIVER AT SULTANPUR.` · `WHAT HAPPENS, WHAT THE BANI SAYS.` · `THE BANI IS THE MEASURE.` · then, large: `WHAT DOES IT KNOW?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what one sakhi teaches. Pick any one we've met this year: milk and jasmine at Multan, the true bargain, the river. Settle and breathe, and let the scene play once. Then set aside whether. Ask only what. What does this story know about God, about people, about how to live? Let the answer come in one short sentence, plain enough to tell a child. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when the sentence arrives. The bell holds the time.
Sakhi, a story of the Guru's life, read not as a news report but as truth in the shape of a story, checked against the Guru's own word.
Your line: what does it know. Today, when a story comes your way, a family tale, a saying, a forwarded message, ask what it knows before you ask whether it's true. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

728.title: Mata Sulakhni and the sons
728.hook: Nanak's wife raised their sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das, while he traveled
728.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Mata Sulakhni as Guru Nanak's wife and the mother of Baba Sri Chand and Baba Lakhmi Das, and remember her in the stories of the Guru's household.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakhi, and your line, what does it know. Did a story come your way that you read for its meaning first? Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

A journey story often has someone just outside the frame. The one who packed the food. The one who watched the road. The one who answered the door when the neighbors came asking where he'd gone. Yesterday we learned to ask what a story knows. The janamsakhis follow Guru Nanak and Mardana down long roads. Today we turn around and look back at the house he left, and at the woman who kept it. Today: Mata Sulakhni.
screen: `SOMEONE JUST OUTSIDE THE FRAME.` → `THE ROAD, AND THE HOUSE.` → `TURN AROUND AND LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: Her name was Sulakhni. Sikhs call her Mata Sulakhni, Mata meaning mother, the honor given to the women of the Gurus' households. She and Nanak had two sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. And when Nanak set out on his long journeys, she stayed. She raised the boys. She kept the household going while Nanak, who had left his post at the storehouse, was on the road. The janamsakhis don't give her many lines. Where she does appear, she's honest. Some tellings show her worry: a husband gone a long time on the road, children growing up with an empty place at the table. Some tellings have her asking him plainly what will become of her and the boys. Notice that the stories keep that question in. They didn't polish it out. Now ask what the story knows. Guru Nanak's own hymns praise the life of the householder, the one who earns honestly, shares, and remembers God in the middle of family life, rather than leaving the world behind. And in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak ends his travels at Kartarpur, back in ordinary clothes, working the fields with his family. So the road came home. And while it was out there, someone at home was living the householder's life that the hymns describe, without a crowd and without a sakhi of her own. Sikhs remember her and honor her name. She is the one who stayed. A long road often has one, and the story goes quiet where they stand.
screen: `MATA SULAKHNI, AND TWO SONS.` · `SHE STAYED AND KEPT THE HOUSE.` · `HER QUESTION STAYS IN THE STORY.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S LIFE, AT HOME.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who kept home going. Settle and breathe. Let one face come to you. A parent who worked the night shift. A grandmother who cooked for everyone. A partner who held things together while you were away, busy, or simply elsewhere. A sibling who stayed close to the family when you moved. Just see them for a moment, doing the ordinary thing they did. Then plan the thanks: a call, a message, a sentence said out loud. Make it specific. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sulakhni, Guru Nanak's wife, who stayed and raised Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das while he traveled.
